facts.statement: Designated as Cave 16, the Kailasa temple is the largest rock-cut Hindu temple among the 34 monuments spanning over two kilometres along the basalt cliff at Ellora.

evidence.quote: UNESCO World Heritage Site #243 (Ellora Caves): These 34 monasteries and temples, extending over more than 2 km, were dug side by side in the wall of a high basalt cliff, not far from Aurangabad, in Maharashtra. Ellora, with its uninterrupted sequence of monuments dating from A.D. 600 to 1000, brings the civilization of ancient India to life. Not only is the Ellora complex a unique artistic creation and a technological exploit but, with its sanctuaries devoted to Buddhism, Hinduism and Jainism, it illustrates the spirit of tolerance that was characteristic of ancient India.

The Kailasha (IAST: Kailāśa) or Kailasha-natha (IAST: Kailāśa-nātha) temple is the largest of the rock-cut Hindu temples at the Ellora Caves in Chhatrapati Sambhaji Nagar district of Maharashtra, India.

The Kailasa temple (Cave 16) is the largest of the 34 Hindu, Buddhist, and Jain cave temples and monasteries known collectively as the Ellora Caves, ranging for over two kilometres (1.2 mi) along the sloping basalt cliff at the site.

facts.statement: Archaeologists determine that the massive cliff-face structure was sculpted entirely out of a single rock.

evidence.quote: A megalith carved into a cliff face, it is considered one of the most remarkable cave temples in the world because of its size, architecture, and sculptural treatment.
Although the rock face slopes downwards from the rear of the temple to the front, archaeologists believe it was sculpted from a single rock.

facts.statement: Builders executed the monument using top-down vertical excavation, carving downward from the summit of the mountain cliff rather than building from the ground up.

evidence.quote: The Kailasa Temple is notable for its vertical excavation—carvers started at the top of the original rock and excavated downward.

facts.statement: Excavating the temple directly as a monolith out of bedrock required less physical effort than transporting large stones to erect a freestanding temple of equal size.

evidence.quote: Moreover, quarrying a monolithic temple would have actually involved less effort than transporting large stones to build a new temple of similar size.

facts.statement: At a cutting rate of four cubic feet of rock per person each day, a workforce of 250 laborers could have carved the Kailasa temple in 5.5 years.
facts.hedge: by one estimate, at a cutting rate of four cubic feet of rock per person each day, a workforce of 250 laborers could have carved the Kailasa temple in 5.5 years.

evidence.quote: Assuming that one person can cut around 4 cubic feet of rock every day, Dhavalikar estimated that 250 labourers would have managed to construct the Kailasa temple at Ellora within 5.5 years.

facts.statement: Architectural evidence demonstrates that the entire monolithic complex was planned from the outset, with no primary structure added as an afterthought.

evidence.quote: Dhavalikar pointed out that no major part of the monolithic temple appears to have been an afterthought: architectural evidence suggests that the entire temple was planned at the beginning.

facts.statement: The primary shrine of Kailasa was constructed utilizing the blueprint and architectural prototype of the Virupaksha Temple at Pattadakal.

evidence.quote: The main shrine is very similar to (although much larger than) the Virupaksha Temple at Pattadakal, which itself is a replica of the Kailasa temple at Kanchi.

If one assumes that the architects of the Virupaksha temple helped construct the Kailasa temple at Ellora, the construction of a massive temple during the reign of a single monarch does not seem impossible.
The architects already had a blueprint and a prototype, which must have significantly reduced the effort involved in constructing a new temple.

facts.statement: The rock-cut temple merges regional engineering traditions by incorporating distinct Chalukya and Pallava artistic styles directly into the monument.

evidence.quote: The temple architecture shows traces of Pallava and Chalukya styles.
The Kailasa temple features the use of several distinct architectural and sculptural styles.
The presence of non-Rashtrakuta styles in the temple can be attributed to the involvement of Chalukya and Pallava artists.

facts.statement: Archaeoastronomical surveys demonstrate that the temple's structural layout incorporates mathematical sacred geometry and a precise solar axis orientation.

evidence.quote: This paper offers a systematic multi domain investigation of astronomical alignment and cosmological context of Kailasa Temple at Ellora.
The study incorporates astronomical alignment, integrating architectural design, sacred geometry, solar axis orientation, an extended analysis of the Nandi Mandapa and ritual timing.
The architectural marvels of Indian temples, particularly from the classical period, exhibit a remarkable integration of mathematics and geometry.

facts.statement: The cosmological design and proportions of the temple reflect classical guidelines outlined in Chapter 56 of the 6th century CE Brihat Samhita.

evidence.quote: Evidence is drawn from epigraphic records, drawing on the primary prescriptive text Varahamihira's Brihat Samhita (6th century CE, Chapter 56), epigraphic records, the peer-reviewed archaeoastronomical study by Vahia, Jamkhedkar and Mahajani (2017), and set up architectural scholarship.

facts.statement: Excavation of the Kailasa temple commenced under the eighth-century Rashtrakuta king Krishna I.
facts.hedge: While traditional scholarship attributes the primary founding of the temple to King Krishna I, competing stylistic analysis suggests excavation began earlier during the reign of Dantidurga.

Based on this, art historian Hermann Goetz (1952) theorized that the construction of the Kailasa temple began during the reign of Dantidurga.

Dhavalikar (1982) analyzed the architecture of the temple, and concluded that the major part of the temple was completed during the reign of Krishna I, although he agreed with Goetz that some other parts of the temple complex can be dated to the later rulers.

facts.statement: Carved into the edifice is a massive relief depicting Ravana shaking Mount Kailasa, considered one of the foremost achievements of Indian rock sculpture.

evidence.quote: Dhavalikar admits that the most important sculpture of the temple, which depicts Ravana shaking the Kailasa mountain, appears to have been built after the main edifice.
This sculpture is considered one of the finest pieces of Indian art, and it is possible that the temple came to be known as Kailasa after it.

facts.statement: A medieval Marathi legend recounts that an architect named Kokasa carved the structure from the summit down so the queen could view the completed shikhara within a week's time.

evidence.quote: A medieval Marathi legend appears to refer to the construction of the Kailasa temple.
She vowed to construct a temple if her wish was granted, and promised to observe a fast until she could see the shikhara (top) of this temple.
One architect named Kokasa assured the king that the queen would be able to see the shikhara of a temple within a week's time.
He started building the temple from the top, by carving a rock.
